hooks.text: Betelgeuse is not quietly waiting to explode in Orion.
Orion's giant shoulder star is actually an interstellar runaway.
Why is Orion's famous shoulder star fleeing into deep space?

title: The Runaway Giant Hiding in Orion
description: Betelgeuse is not merely waiting to go supernova—it is an interstellar runaway star hurtling through space at 30 kilometers per second.

beats.text: Betelgeuse is not quietly waiting to explode in Orion.
beats.visual: Hubble Space Telescope image of Betelgeuse's glowing atmosphere, 1995

beats.text: Many assume this famous red supergiant sits motionless, simply counting down roughly 100,000 years to its demise.
beats.visual: Night sky astrophotograph showing the constellation Orion with reddish Betelgeuse, 2020

beats.text: At roughly 10 million years old, it is bloated enough to swallow the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.
beats.visual: Diagram comparing Betelgeuse's diameter to the orbits of inner solar system planets, 2009

beats.text: Yet this giant was violently ejected from its stellar birthplace near Orion's Belt.
beats.visual: Deep field photograph of the Orion Nebula and Orion's Belt stars, 2017

beats.text: Betelgeuse is an interstellar runaway, plowing through the interstellar medium at 30 kilometers per second.
beats.visual: Artist impression of runaway star Betelgeuse racing through interstellar gas, 2013

beats.text: Crashing through cosmic gas at that breakneck speed creates a massive bow shock.
beats.visual: Herschel Space Observatory infrared image of Betelgeuse's curved bow shock, 2013

beats.text: When it finally detonates, its daytime explosion will leave life on Earth completely unharmed.
beats.visual: Illustration of a brilliant daytime supernova shining beside the Moon, 2021

beats.text: Few realize Orion's brightest shoulder is actually fleeing across deep space, proving
beats.visual: Wide-angle photograph of the constellation Orion over Cerro Paranal, 2019
